description: Create django-backend and deploy skills so Django and deploy specifics load on demand rather than sitting in always-loaded context. Symlink .claude/skills -> ../.agents/skills for Claude Code discovery; verify Claude follows a symlinked skills dir.
close_reason: Closed

title: Add Docker + devcontainer infra for backend
description: Create backend/Dockerfile, .dockerignore, compose.yaml and .devcontainer/devcontainer.json so README deploy instructions and DEVELOPERS setup describe something real. mise.toml already pulls devcontainer-cli.
close_reason: Closed

title: Write README.md with usage and deploy instructions
description: User-and-operator facing doc: what inventory-tng is, prerequisites, quickstart, and deployment via the container image (env vars, migrations, serving, collectstatic).
close_reason: Closed

title: Group a multi-issue batch under an epic
description:
DEVELOPERS.md#pull-requests requires a batch of more than one issue to be grouped under an epic 'so that what belongs to it is recorded rather than remembered'. Pull request 7 landed four issues -- 2zx, kx6, a7j and hr2 -- with no epic and no parent edges, while every earlier multi-issue batch has one (c6j, c6b, 2lo, 8fp, z6t).

scripts/check-batch.sh passes because with no epic there is no membership to check, which is the wrong way round: the absence of the grouping is exactly what should fail. Either the checker gains that check or the rule is relaxed deliberately, but the current state means a batch can skip it silently.
acceptance_criteria: A multi-issue batch without an epic is either impossible or reported, and the decision between those two is recorded.
close_reason: batch-membership.py refuses a multi-issue range with no epic, with a test case; the rule is enforced rather than remembered.

title: Say every over-long body line, not just the first
description:
check-commit.sh breaks out of the body-width loop after the first line over 72 columns, so a message with three long lines takes three runs to fix. Every other rule it checks reports in full.

Noticed while landing inventory-tng-spk: three round trips for one message, and the third only because the second fix was written by hand against a report that named one line.
close_reason: Every over-long body line is reported in one run, with each shown, rather than the first and a break.

title: An epic's closure counts as work it never did
description:
check-commit.sh refuses a commit whose staged tracker moves two issues to closed. That is right for work, and wrong for an epic: an epic groups a batch and carries no work of its own, so closing it alongside the last bead of its batch is bookkeeping, not a second unit.

Today the only ways out are to leave the epic open after its batch merges, or to give its closure a commit of its own -- which then has a Closes trailer for something nobody implemented.

Ignore issues of type epic when counting closures, and say so in DEVELOPERS.md Commits. bd epic close-eligible already knows when one is finished.

Noticed while landing inventory-tng-b8n, when the batch-1 epic's close collided with it.
close_reason: An epic is not counted as a closure: it groups a batch and does no work of its own.

title: The read boundary is a glob, not the principle
description:
DEVELOPERS.md states the line well: a script header documents the repository and is where a guide's explanation gets re-derived, while a docstring beside the invariant it enforces is code explaining itself. check-docs.sh implements that as scripts/*.sh and scripts/*.py, which is a location rather than the distinction.

By the stated test, batch-membership.py and ci-check-names.py are helpers whose docstrings are code explaining itself, and they are read; .github/workflows/ci.yml, whose comments repo-settings.sh's whole design depends on, is not. Move a helper out of scripts/ and it stops being checked, with no signal.

Raised by the simplify pass on pull request 2. Related to inventory-tng-lwe.
close_reason: The boundary is an exclusion of application source, so a file added or moved is read by default; workflows and the chart are read now.

title: Make the message rules a module, not a subprocess to scrape
description:
check-batch.sh delegates the message rules to check-commit.sh by forking it once per commit and grepping the failure glyph out of its stdout, then re-wrapping each scraped line with the commit's short sha. Two scripts that sit beside each other and already source a shared library are talking over stdout text, and the re-wrap flattens any objection that runs to two lines.

Delegating is right -- the rules must have one home, and a subprocess guarantees a contributor's hook and CI enforce identical text. The mechanism is what is a layer too low. A sourced module holding the rules as functions, with check-commit.sh as the command-line interface over it, removes the scraping and the fork per commit.

Raised by the simplify pass on pull request 2.
close_reason: The message rules are scripts/message-rules.sh, sourced by both checkers; check-batch.sh calls them instead of forking check-commit.sh and grepping its stdout.

title: The new receipt file is not ignored
description:
.gitignore lists .claude/.landing-receipt.json, which the landing gate stopped writing when inventory-tng-c6j.8 reworked it to key receipts on the pull request. It now writes .claude/.review-receipts.json, which nothing ignores, so it shows up as untracked in every git status and is one 'git add -A' away from being committed.

Local machinery, like the hook that writes it, and should be ignored the same way.
close_reason: One pattern matches whatever the local gate calls its receipt, rather than listing a name that has already changed once.

title: Read application code comments for duplicated prose too
description:
check-docs.sh reads Markdown and the headers of scripts/. Pointing it at backend/ and frontend/ as well finds 64 more passages living in two places, most of them a model or view docstring reproducing docs/data-model.md or a decision record, and tests restating the module they test.

They are real by the letter of the rule, but they are a different genre from a topic having two homes: a docstring beside the invariant it enforces is the code explaining itself. Each needs deciding on its own -- some should be deleted and linked, some are the right kind of repetition and want an allowance naming the pair.

Sixty-four judgements is a batch, not a step in the issue that widened the input set. Raised while doing inventory-tng-5yf.
acceptance_criteria: check-docs.sh reads backend/ and frontend/ comments, and the repository passes with an allowlist whose every entry is justified.

title: Name the CI jobs for what they now do
description:
The commit-check job is still called 'Commit checker' while running four checker suites, and the docs job is still 'Documentation links' while also running the duplication check. Both names describe what the job was when it had one step.

Renaming used to be dangerous: the required-check names were hardcoded in repo-settings.sh, so a rename silently un-required the job on main. They are now read out of ci.yml, so a rename is safe as long as repo-settings.sh is rerun -- which is the point of deriving them.
close_reason: Commit checker is Guardrail checkers; Documentation links is Documentation. Safe because the required-check names are read out of ci.yml.

title: Stop hand-maintaining the batch list in the template
description:
The pull request template asks for a table of the issues in the batch and a checkbox asserting every commit holds exactly one issue. Both are facts the machinery already owns: the epic records membership, batch-membership.py verifies it against the branch, and the required 'One issue per commit' check decides the proposition the checkbox asserts.

Pull request 1 proved the cost -- inventory-tng-724 joined the batch late and the table went stale with nothing to notice. A ticked box asserting a machine-checked fact also trains people to tick boxes.

Drop both. If the membership belongs in the pull request, have the history job post what check-batch.sh already knows, so the list is verified rather than typed.
close_reason: The template stops asking for the batch list and the machine-checked checkbox; the history job posts what check-batch.sh --list read off the commits.

title: The tracker diff is read twice on every commit
description:
check-commit.sh runs git diff --cached over .beads/issues.jsonl twice: once to find what closed, once with --name-only to ask whether the path was staged at all. The first diff already answers the second question by being empty or not.

This runs as a commit-msg hook on every local commit against a 180KB tracker. Predates the pull-request-workflow batch, so it was not fixed there.

Raised by the simplify pass on pull request 1.
close_reason: One git diff, used for both questions: what closed, and whether the tracker was staged at all.

title: Nothing runs the settings check
description:
repo-settings.sh exists because settings left as something somebody once clicked drift unnoticed. The remedy shipped is a script run by hand plus a sentence telling you to remember to run it, so the failure mode survives one level up: protection can be relaxed in the web UI and main will accept things it should not, with no signal.

enforce_admins, allow_force_pushes and required_linear_history are exactly the settings that cannot be enforced from the repository, so their silent loss is the most expensive drift available. A weekly scheduled workflow running --check would catch it; it needs a token with Administration: read.

Raised by the simplify pass on pull request 1.
close_reason: A weekly scheduled job runs repo-settings.sh --check, and any pull request touching CI's job names runs it too.

title: An allowance should name the pair it was granted for
description:
check-docs.sh's is_allowed tests containment against every allowed passage regardless of which files collided. Once README.md and 0008 are allowed, the same passage appearing in a fourth file is permitted too, silently and forever.

Make an entry name its two files plus the passage. A third copy then fails, and an allowance that matched nothing can be reported as dead -- which makes the baseline self-deleting rather than permanent.

Raised by the simplify pass on pull request 1.
close_reason: An allowance names the two files it covers; a third copy is refused, and an allowance matching nothing is reported so the baseline cannot outlive its debt.

title: Two passages live in two files
description:
check-docs.sh found two explanations pasted into a second file, both predating it, so they are baselined in scripts/check-docs.allow rather than fixed under the issue that added the checker:

- README.md and docs/decisions/0008 on why a correction cannot be expressed
- docs/briefs/authorisation.md and docs/decisions/0014 on signing in not navigating

For each, decide which file owns it, delete the other copy, link instead, and remove its line from the allowlist. A brief is the investigation and the decision is the conclusion, so the decision most likely owns it.
close_reason: README defers to 0008 for the correction evidence; the authorisation brief defers to 0014 for what one interface means. The allowlist is empty.

title: A scanner that has stopped reading looks exactly like a shelf with no labels on it
description:
frontend/src/scan/decodeLoop.ts reads a rejected decode as 'no code in this frame', which is right for the ordinary case -- most frames are a shelf, or a label mid-focus -- and wrong for the permanent one. A detector whose every call throws (an unbound method, a detached ArrayBuffer, a WASM heap that will not grow, a tainted canvas) is indistinguishable from a volunteer pointing the phone at nothing: the preview is live and moving, the loop keeps ticking five times a second, and there is no message, no console output and no counter anywhere that says the scanner is dead.

The same gap has a second half. `frame()` and `onCode()` are deliberately left OUTSIDE the swallow, on the argument that a bug there should surface rather than hide -- but nothing surfaces it either. The interval callback is async and its promise is unhandled, so what actually happens is an unhandled rejection five times a second for as long as the camera is open, which no error boundary sees and no volunteer is told about.

WHAT TO DECIDE

This is a product decision before it is a code one, which is why it is not a review fix:

- How many consecutive failures mean 'stopped' rather than 'unlucky'? At 5 Hz even a second of failures is five.
- What does the volunteer see? Something like 'the scanner has stopped reading -- close and reopen the camera, or type the code printed under the QR' names a way out, which is the standard the rest of scan/ holds itself to (see NO_CAMERA and refusal() in CameraScanner.tsx).
- Does the loop stop itself at that point, or keep trying? Keeping the lens powered for a loop that cannot decode costs battery for nothing.

Whatever is decided, the failure has to leave the loop by a route the component can see -- an onFailure alongside onCode is the obvious shape -- rather than being counted inside a module that has no screen.

Raised by the xhigh review of inventory-tng-w1e, which found both halves and correctly declined to invent the policy.
acceptance_criteria: A detector that fails repeatedly stops being read as an empty shelf: the volunteer is told the scanner has stopped reading and what to do instead, and a frame source or onCode that throws no longer escapes as an unhandled rejection. Both paths tested in decodeLoop.test.ts.
close_reason: A run of refusals stops the loop and tells the volunteer; a frame source or onCode that throws does the same instead of becoming an unhandled rejection.

title: CameraScanner is 68% covered, and most of the gap is testable
description:
CameraScanner.tsx sits at 68% lines while the rest of the frontend is 95-100%, and it is the single reason the project total is 94.8% rather than ~97%. The uncovered block is lines 135-182 and 192: everything from getUserMedia resolving through to the decode loop and its teardown.

It was left that way on the judgement that covering it means faking a camera, which would prove the fakes work rather than the code. That judgement is right about faking the DECODE and wrong about faking the LIFECYCLE, which was not checked at the time. It has now been checked.

WHAT WAS MEASURED

A throwaway test of about twenty lines -- stubbing navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia and enumerateDevices, and spying HTMLMediaElement.prototype.play -- rendered the component, ran open() to completion, and on unmount the fake track's stop() was genuinely called. That single test covered 48.68% of the file on its own. So the stream lifecycle is reachable in jsdom today with no new tooling.

Where it stops is loadDetector(), which dynamically imports the real WebAssembly module; under Node that fails on the wasm URL. Past that point the decode loop is reachable only with vi.mock of ./decoder.

THE THREE BANDS, AND WHICH DESERVE A TEST

1. getUserMedia -> srcObject -> play() -> listCameras -> teardown. Reachable now. A test here asserts our own rules, not a fake's behaviour: that the stream is assigned before play, that every track is stopped on cleanup, and that a stream or a timer arriving AFTER teardown is still released. Two of those were real bugs a review caught, so they have earned tests.

2. The decode loop, with a faked detector. Also our own rules: skip while busy, recheck live after the await, hand every code in a frame to onCode, treat a decode failure as the ordinary case rather than an error. The post-await live recheck was itself a bug found in review -- a decode landing after the volunteer closed the scanner added a line to the batch.

3. That zxing actually reads a QR from a real frame. NOT this bead. No test here may claim it, and a fake detector returning a canned rawValue must not be dressed up as proof of decoding. That is inventory-tng-qsu.

APPROACH

Prefer extracting band 2 over stubbing it in place. The loop's policy is a function of an injected detect, an injected frame source and an injected liveness check; pulled into its own module it is plainly unit-testable, and the component drops to wiring -- the same move that produced frame.ts, cameras.ts, confirm.ts and decoder.ts, and the reason those are all covered while this file is not. Band 1 stays in the component, tested with the stubs above, because it is about the component.

Coverage is the side effect here, not the goal. A pile of stubs in CameraScanner.test.tsx would reach a similar number without the improvement; that is not what this bead asks for.

NOT ACCEPTABLE AS A SOLUTION: a coverage exclusion (the project forbids one), moving the file out of the include glob, or lowering the threshold. Whether the 90% gate should be per-directory rather than global is a fair question but a separate one -- the frontend currently has about 29 lines of headroom, and the next untestable browser API could fail the build for a reason that is not a quality regression.

RELATIONSHIP TO inventory-tng-qsu: if this lands first, that bead gets smaller. Its job narrows to the one assertion only a real browser can make -- that a real frame carrying a real symbol produces a cart line -- because everything around it will already be covered here.

Raised from a question about why frontend coverage sits below the backend's.
acceptance_criteria: The decode loop's policy is tested independently of any real camera or decoder, and the stream lifecycle is tested through the component, including that a stream or timer arriving after teardown is released. No test claims to prove that a QR code decodes. No coverage exclusion is added.
close_reason: The decode loop is now its own module with its own tests, and the stream lifecycle is tested through the component. CameraScanner.tsx went 68% -> 100%, the frontend 94.8% -> 98.9% lines, with no coverage exclusion. Two things the work found: the post-loop 'if (!live) release()' was unreachable (nothing awaits between it and the check above), and a stream granted before a later failure was never released at all -- both fixed. inventory-tng-spk was raised for the decoder's poisoned promise, which is decoder.ts's own bug.

title: Leftovers from the batch-3 simplify pass
description:
Small items found by the reuse and simplification reviews of inventory-tng-p3t, ea6 and vci, judged real but left for later so the batch could land. None changes behaviour.

1. frontend/src/scan/: the label fixtures (PACKET, WALL, a cable label) and the "two reads a code costs" fetch stub are copy-pasted into DeepLink.test.tsx, Scanner.test.tsx and applyCode.test.ts. scan/testFixtures.ts already exists for this directory and holds only the camera fixtures. A field added to ResolvedLabel is four edits.

2. frontend/src/batch/movements.ts: movementFor() calls sideFor(cart.kind) inside the map and re-checks cart.locationId per line, though both are constant for the batch. Compute once in batchBody and pass it.

3. frontend/src/storage.ts: isText is typed as returning boolean rather than as a "value is string" type predicate, which is the only reason cameras.ts declares its own inline predicate. Widening it satisfies the Shape type unchanged.

4. frontend/src/scan/outcome.tsx exports announcement(), which nothing outside the file imports.

5. frontend/src/scan/Scanner.tsx has a .catch on the applyCode promise that is unreachable as written -- no signal is passed and applyCode answers rather than throws -- so it now only swallows genuine bugs.

Each is a few lines. Worth doing together rather than one at a time.
acceptance_criteria: All five are addressed or each one that is not has a reason recorded here.
notes:
Item 5 was NOT done, and the reason is that the bead's premise was wrong. The .catch on the applyCode promise is reachable: DeepLink passes an AbortSignal and aborts it on unmount, so an abandoned deep-link scan lands there. useScannedCode's comment already says so. The other four are done.

Item 1 landed in two halves: the label fixtures (PACKET, WALL, CABLE_LABEL) and the fetch stub (serving, refusing) both live in scan/testFixtures.ts now. A review caught that consolidating the fixtures had given WALL and the cable label the same code, which was invisible while they lived in separate files; WALL now has its own.
close_reason: Closed

title: Nothing verifies the label decoder is served from our own origin
description:
inventory-tng-p3t's acceptance criteria include 'the wasm asset is served from our own origin' -- a non-optional constraint from decision 0011 section 2, because the page has to work in a basement and the frontend image is self-contained.

What exists today: a unit test asserting locateFile() returns a non-http(s) path, and a manual check of the build output. What does not exist is anything that fails when the assertion stops being true. The jsdelivr URL is still present in the ponyfill chunk as zxing-wasm's dead default, so a regression that let it be used would look exactly like today's build to every automated check.

frontend/integration/ is the right home: a Playwright test that opens the camera and asserts every request for a .wasm went to the page's own origin -- and that none went to a CDN. The agent that built the scanner left it out because integration/ was outside its file scope, and said so.

Raised by a review of inventory-tng-p3t.
acceptance_criteria: A test fails if the decoder binary is fetched from anywhere but the origin serving the app.
close_reason: Closed

title: The explanation for a missing camera is unreachable by the person who needs it
description:
frontend/src/scan/Scanner.tsx renders the Camera button only when cameraSupported() is true, and the "camera" state can only become true through that button. CameraScanner.tsx then checks cameraSupported() again and, when false, renders a 40-word message naming the commonest real cause -- that the page was reached over plain HTTP at a LAN address, which is why getUserMedia is not there.

That message can never be seen by a volunteer. They get a silently missing button instead, on exactly the setup where the explanation would tell them what to do. The branch is reached only by CameraScanner.test.tsx.

Two ways out, and they are opposite: drop the guard in CameraScanner so one place decides, or drop Scanner gate so the explanation reaches the person who needs it. The second is what the message was written for.

Raised by a review of inventory-tng-p3t.
acceptance_criteria: A volunteer on a device or origin where the camera cannot work is told why, rather than shown nothing. Only one place decides whether the camera is on offer.
close_reason: Closed

title: Every cart change re-renders every catalogue row
description:
frontend/src/items/ItemRow.tsx is not memoized -- there is no React.memo anywhere in frontend/src -- and CartProvider hands a new context value on every cart change. So one scan re-renders all 50 rows of the page, each rebuilding a Set and sorting it in packetSizes(), running a reduce in onHand(), and doing a linear cart.lines.find().

Measured in jsdom with 50 rows: a keystroke-triggered re-render costs about 30 ms; wrapping the export in React.memo drops it to 2.5-4.6 ms, roughly 7x, because data.results object identities are unchanged until a new response arrives. It does not help the cart-dispatch render, which is a context update and bypasses memo -- that one wants the per-row work hoisted or memoized instead.

Pre-existing rather than introduced by any one bead: it was measured during a review of inventory-tng-p3t, on code from inventory-tng-6su.

Note the related finding already fixed: CartProvider's dispatch is now stable across cart changes, so an effect depending on it no longer re-runs per scan.
acceptance_criteria: A cart change does not rebuild the packaging chips and balances of every row on the page. The measurement that justifies whatever is done is in the test or a comment.
close_reason: Closed

title: The camera decode loop allocates a canvas and two full-frame buffers per tick
description:
frontend/src/scan/CameraScanner.tsx passes the HTMLVideoElement straight to detector.detect(), which takes barcode-detector's slow path: it allocates a NEW OffscreenCanvas and 2D context on every call (never reused), draws the frame, and getImageData's it back from the GPU into a fresh Uint8ClampedArray of width*height*4. zxing-wasm then runs a plain-JS per-pixel loop into another width*height grayscale buffer and memcpys that into the WASM heap.

Measured at 640x480 and the loop's 5 Hz: about 7.7 MB/s of garbage, 1.5 M JS loop iterations per second, and 5 GPU readbacks per second. constraints() in cameras.ts asks for no width/height, so a device that answers 1280x720 makes all of it 4x -- and nothing in the code knows which it got. This is the battery cost DECODE_INTERVAL_MS's comment is trying to bound, and it is unbounded in the dimension that matters.

The fix: keep one canvas in a ref, drawImage scaled to a fixed working size (~640 on the long edge), getImageData from that, and hand the resulting ImageData to detect() -- which then takes the fast path and allocates nothing of its own. That caps the pixel count whatever the camera returns and removes the per-tick canvas. Adding width: { ideal: 1280 } to constraints() would at least make the cost knowable.

Raised by a review of inventory-tng-p3t and measured against the installed barcode-detector/zxing-wasm.
acceptance_criteria: One canvas is reused across ticks and the decoded frame is a bounded size whatever resolution the camera returns. The measured per-tick allocation is stated in a comment so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.
notes:
Done, with one limit worth knowing: per-tick allocation is reduced, not removed. getImageData must return a fresh ImageData each tick, so about 5.8 MB/s at 640x360 remains, against 7.7 MB/s at 640x480 before and roughly three times that from an unconstrained 720p phone. What is gone outright is the per-tick canvas and 2D context, and the growth with whatever resolution the camera chose.

A review noted that constraints() now asks width ideal 1280, which raises as well as lowers: a laptop webcam that would have answered 640x480 is now asked for 720p, so the drawImage that frame.ts cannot avoid got larger on exactly the devices that were already cheap. Kept because the preview and autofocus are worth it, and said so in the docstring rather than left as an accident.
close_reason: Closed

title: LabelSheetView inherits ListAPIView to answer with a document
description:
GET /api/labels/sheet answers with an HTML page, not a list of rows, and four accommodations stack up to make a list view do that:

- list() is overridden not to serialize
- serializer_class is set to a serializer the code itself documents as never rendering anything, because ListAPIView asks for one
- filterset_class declares a 'code' parameter drf-spectacular cannot read for a non-list operation, so the parameter is re-declared by hand in @extend_schema
- LabelSheetRenderer has to know DRF's {'detail': ...} error shape in order to render a refusal as a page

Staying inside DRF is right and should not change: permissions, throttles, the exception handler and open_to_anybody all come free, and the HTML media type is deliberate (a JSON body of SVG strings would put the dimensions that decide whether a label scans on the far side of the API from the tests that assert them).

What is wrong is the base class. An APIView with a get() that reads 'code' off query_params, filters LIVE_LABELS and returns HttpResponse(sheet(...), content_type='text/html') drops all four: DRF's finalize_response passes a non-Response through untouched. The one thing worth keeping is the HTML-rendered 403, which becomes a small handle_exception override rather than a renderer class.

Raised by a review of inventory-tng-n2o. Not urgent -- the endpoint works and is tested -- but the comment in views.py now points here rather than justifying the field.
acceptance_criteria: The sheet endpoint carries no serializer it does not use and no hand-written duplicate of a parameter its filter declares, and the refusal is still an HTML page. Tests unchanged in what they assert.
close_reason: Closed

title: The schema does not describe the 400 a refused write answers with
description:
PolicyAwareAutoSchema (backend/src/inventory/api.py) derives 403, 404 and 429 from the view's own policy, but nothing derives 400. So none of the catalogue write operations publishes a shape for the validation refusals its serializers produce, even though inventory-tng-0rr added validators specifically so a client would get a 400 naming the field rather than a 500 naming nothing.

A client generated from openapi.yaml has no type for the body of POST /api/items with reorder_quantity 0, POST /api/locations with a custody location and no holder, or PATCH /api/categories/{id} with a looping parent.

The contract is also inconsistent with itself: POST /api/stock/transactions documents its 400 explicitly, through BatchRejectedSerializer, because its body is bespoke -- a flat list of errors carrying the index of the offending line.

What needs deciding is the shape to publish for the ordinary case. DRF renders a field map, {field: [messages]}, plus non_field_errors for complaints about the body as a whole. That is not expressible as a Serializer's own fields, so it needs either a hand-written OpenApiResponse with additionalProperties, or a decision to give the catalogue writes the same flat errors array the batch endpoint uses -- which would be one error shape across the whole API and is probably the better answer, at the cost of changing a response clients already read.

Raised by a review of inventory-tng-0rr.
acceptance_criteria: Every operation that can answer 400 describes the body it answers with, and the description is generated rather than repeated per view. A decision records whether the API has one error shape or two.
notes:
Decision: the API keeps two error shapes, and this bead describes both rather than unifying them.

Considered: giving the catalogue writes the flat {detail, errors: [{index, field, detail}]} body the batch endpoint uses, so the whole API had one error shape. Rejected:

1. It changes a response clients already read. The bead is about the schema being silent, not about the body being wrong; DRF renders the field map today and a client written against a running server already handles it. Changing it would be a breaking change made in passing, in a bead whose acceptance criterion is a description.
2. The two shapes are not describing the same thing. A batch is refused line by line and a line is identified by its position in the submitted array; a map keyed by field name has nowhere to put an index, so unifying downward loses information. Unifying upward -- giving every single-row write an index that is always null -- pays that cost on eleven operations to spare one.
3. The field map is what DRF produces unaided. Adopting the flat shape everywhere means an exception handler or a per-view wrapper on every catalogue write, so the API would carry code to make its refusals uniform rather than carry a schema that says what they are.

Implemented instead: PolicyAwareAutoSchema derives 400 the way it already derives 403, 404 and 429 -- from the operation having a request body to refuse -- and publishes a ValidationError component (object, additionalProperties: array of string). setdefault leaves POST /api/stock/transactions its BatchRejected. If one shape is wanted later it is a versioned change of its own, with the frontend in scope.
close_reason: Closed

title: No test renders an admin page, because staticfiles has no manifest under test
description:
Decision 0014 point 4 keeps the Django admin as the fallback that works when the single-page app does not. A test now proves every model is registered, but nothing proves a page actually renders.

An attempt to add one failed with ValueError: Missing staticfiles manifest entry for 'admin/css/base.css'. Whitenoise's manifest storage expects collectstatic to have run, which the test environment does not do. The deployed image does collect static, so this is a test-environment gap rather than an admin defect -- but it means the only existing admin test (in test_models.py) POSTs and asserts a 302, never rendering a template.

So a changelist that raises on render -- a stale list_display naming a removed field, a broken __str__, a bad ModelAdmin method -- would pass every test we have. Django's own checks framework catches some of that (checks.run_checks(tags=['admin']) is now run), but not everything that only appears at render time.

The fix is a test-settings override of STORAGES for staticfiles, which touches settings.py. Found by the agent implementing inventory-tng-cck, which left it alone rather than reach outside its file scope.
acceptance_criteria: A test renders the changelist and change form of every registered model and fails if either raises.
close_reason: Closed

title: Device enrolment for volunteers: registered keys and signed requests
description:
Decision 0012 point 4, deferred until the volunteer flow is in real use and the cost of enrolment friction is known.

The shape: on first use the browser generates a keypair it cannot export (WebCrypto, extractable false, handle in IndexedDB), registers the public half against a secret printed on the wall poster or an administrator's approval, and signs every request with it under RFC 9421. Turns 'anyone who can reach the API' into 'anyone who has been in the room'.

Enrolling needs no camera: the secret is a string, and the Crockford alphabet decision 0011 already specifies exists so a hand-typed code resolves. A link works too, and 'request access' with administrator approval needs no secret at all.

Known limit, worth stating before anyone starts: a non-exportable key stops the credential being stolen, but script running on the app's own origin can use it as a signing oracle. Device binding raises the cost of theft; it does not make cross-site scripting survivable.

Reading:
- RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html -- one scheme for browsers and machine clients alike; section 1.4 on what a browser can and cannot sign
- Device Bound Session Credentials https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/device-bound-session-credentials -- the browser-native form, GA in Chrome on Windows since April 2026; building the device model first makes adopting it additive
- The DPoP Storage Paradox https://www.infoq.com/articles/dpop-key-storage-unsolved-problem/ -- the signing-oracle limit
- Good Practices for Capability URLs https://www.w3.org/2001/tag/doc/capability-urls -- the secret on the poster

Needs its own decision record when it is picked up.
acceptance_criteria: A device enrols once and signs subsequent requests; a request without a valid signature is refused; enrolment works by typing, by link and by administrator approval; a decision record covers the choices made.

title: Restrict the administrative routes at the network
description:
Decision 0013 point 6. Administrators are few and their locations predictable, unlike volunteers, who are on a phone wherever the stock happens to be. Restricting the administrative routes to the mesh, a VPN or an identity-aware proxy costs those few people very little, and it is the one place a network boundary fits without excluding the person this project exists to serve.

Expressed in the ingress and the network rather than in the application, so its absence is not something the code can detect. That makes it a stated precondition in docs/deployment.md, alongside the existing one about the ingress being the only route to the frontend pod.

Not before the rest of 0012 to 0014: this narrows who can reach a surface that has to exist and be correct first.
acceptance_criteria: The administrative routes are unreachable from outside the permitted network in a deployed environment, and docs/deployment.md states the precondition and how to configure it.
close_reason: Closed

title: Volunteer search matches only the display name, not the identifiers that disambiguate
description:
VolunteerSerializer carries email and slack_id with the reason stated in its docstring: two people called Sean are why the list is searched before anyone adds themselves, and without something to tell them apart the picker cannot help.

But VolunteerFilter.by_name searches display_name alone. A volunteer who types their own email address finds nobody and adds a duplicate -- the exact outcome the endpoint exists to prevent, arrived at through the field that was added to prevent it.

Widening the filter to email and slack_id is a few lines. Worth deciding at the same time whether the picker should search them, or only display them once a name match is found, since an email is not what somebody types when looking for themselves in a list.

Found by a review of inventory-tng-hd0.
acceptance_criteria: Searching by an identifier the serializer exposes finds the volunteer holding it, or a decision records why only names are searched.
close_reason: Closed

title: What active=False means for stock that is still on the shelf
description:
Item.active and Location.active retire a row without deleting its ledger history. Nothing says what that means for stock the retired row still holds, and the two halves of the API now answer differently by omission:

READ. /api/items and /api/locations both hide inactive rows, matching the volunteer pick-list. So a volunteer cannot see, and therefore cannot count or move, stock that is physically on a shelf under a retired item or in a decommissioned room.

WRITE. POST /api/stock/transactions filters the actor to a selectable volunteer but accepts any item, from_location and to_location. So a retired item CAN be recorded against -- just not found through the read API -- and it then reappears in the inventory_stock_balance view with a non-zero quantity.

The asymmetry needs deciding rather than assuming, and the two directions are not the same question: draining an inactive location while decommissioning it is legitimate, moving stock INTO one is not. A retired item is probably never a legitimate target either way, but its remaining stock still has to be countable off the shelf.

Raised by reviews of inventory-tng-hgm and inventory-tng-eg8.
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded about what active=False means for reading and for writing, and both halves of the API match it. If retired rows need to be reachable for a stock count, the read API offers a way that is not a guess.
close_reason: Decision 0019: retirement takes a row out of the pick-list and says nothing about its stock. Stock may leave a retired location and may not arrive, enforced by trigger; the read half was already ?withdrawn=true.

title: Batch validation resolves item and location one query per line
description:
StockMovementInputSerializer resolves item, from_location and to_location through PrimaryKeyRelatedField, whose to_internal_value does get(pk=...) per value. A 24-line transfer therefore costs up to 72 sequential SELECTs before a single row is written, and MAX_MOVEMENTS=500 admits up to 1500 -- against a request whose actual write is two statements. A real cart repeats the same handful of items and one or two locations, so nearly all of them are duplicates of each other.

This is the endpoint the project exists for, and it is used from a phone whose connectivity where stock is kept is unmeasured (ADR 0011 context), so latency here is worth caring about.

Two shapes: resolve in bulk in StockTransactionCreateSerializer.validate (collect every item and location id across the lines, two filter(pk__in=...) queries, report unknown ids by index through the existing error envelope, build movements with item_id=/from_location_id=); or a smaller PrimaryKeyRelatedField subclass memoising lookups across the batch, which collapses 3N to one per distinct id for much less change.

Raised by a review of inventory-tng-hgm; not done there because it restructures validation and its error reporting.
acceptance_criteria: Posting a batch of N lines over M distinct items and locations issues a number of validation queries proportional to M, not N. Unknown ids are still reported by line index. Existing endpoint tests pass unchanged.
close_reason: TLS is no longer a chart toggle and rendering without a certificate fails; batch validation now resolves each distinct id once, taking a 24-line cart from 81 queries to 12

title: API rules with no database counterpart
description:
Several rules the API enforces mirror no database constraint, so anything writing past the serializers and views -- the admin, a fixture load, the planned sheet importer -- is not held to them.

1. The kind-to-sides rule. KIND_SIDES in backend/src/inventory/views.py says which sides each movement kind must carry and which it must not: a checkout needs a from_location, a receipt needs a to_location and must NOT carry a from_location, consumption must not carry a to_location, a transfer needs both (ADR 0011 section 6). Every other per-line rule the serializer reports mirrors a real CheckConstraint. This one mirrors nothing, so another writer can record a receipt that drains a warehouse, and the ledger is append-only so it stands until somebody compensates it. Being cross-table (StockMovement rows against their StockTransaction's kind) it needs a trigger rather than a CheckConstraint, which is why it ended up in the view.
2. occurred_at may not be in the future. Not expressible as a CheckConstraint because timezone.now() is not immutable; it would need a trigger too.
3. The actor must be a selectable volunteer -- neither merged nor inactive. Cross-table, so a trigger again.
4. Location.held_by must be a selectable volunteer. Same shape as 3, and the case that matters: a custody location attached to a merged duplicate is the second generation of the duplicate the merge existed to remove. Enforced only in LocationSerializer.validate_held_by.
5. Volunteer.merged_into must point at a selectable volunteer. Same shape again; without it a merge chain forms and, worse, a cycle can be built. Enforced only in VolunteerDetailSerializer.validate_merged_into.
6. Label.code may not change once printed. The code is on a sticker already on a shelf, so changing it 404s that sticker forever. Needs the row's previous value, so a trigger. Enforced only in LabelSerializer.get_fields.
7. Label.revoked_at is the server's clock, never the client's. Same shape as 2. Enforced only in LabelSerializer.validate.

Items 3, 4 and 5 are one rule -- 'this must be a volunteer the list still offers' -- and one trigger closes all three. 2 and 7 are one rule about time. 6 is its own.

Raised across reviews of inventory-tng-hgm and inventory-tng-6c0, and extended by the review of inventory-tng-0rr, which added items 4 to 7.
acceptance_criteria: Either triggers enforce these for every writer, with migrations and tests, or a decision records why they are client contracts rather than ledger invariants and the serializers.py module docstring stops implying otherwise.
notes:
Item 6 has moved and grown since this was written, per a review of inventory-tng-n2o:

- The immutability rule is no longer in LabelSerializer.get_fields (that method is gone). It is now in LabelSerializer.validate, via _submitted(), AND a second time in LabelAdmin.get_readonly_fields. Two copies of a rule the database cannot hold is exactly what this bead exists to record.
- Rule 4 grew a second half that is NOT on this list: a client may not CHOOSE a code at all -- minting is the server's. The database cannot enforce that one either, because the admin legitimately supplies codes (it is another authorised writer, not a client).

So item 6 should read: a label's code is minted by the server, and is immutable once printed. Enforced in LabelSerializer.validate and LabelAdmin, nowhere below.
close_reason: Closed

title: Should Label.quantity be NULL on a location label rather than pinned to 1
description:
ADR 0011 section 5 chose to pin Label.quantity to 1 on a location label 'rather than left to mean nothing', citing location_held_by_iff_custody as the pattern it follows. But that constraint resolves the same problem the other way: held_by is NULL when the column does not apply, not a sentinel value.

Cost of the pin: every location-label row stores a number that reads as a real multiplier. GET /api/labels/{code} returns quantity for both label kinds, and the packaging chips derive from 'the distinct quantities on an item's active labels', so each consumer must know out-of-band that 1 means 'not applicable' when the label names a location.

The alternative shape: quantity nullable, with an iff-presence constraint (quantity IS NOT NULL exactly when item IS NOT NULL) plus quantity IS NULL OR quantity > 0. A wall code then serialises as null and no client needs the convention.

Raised by a review of inventory-tng-twf. Not acted on because it amends a decision record rather than an implementation.
acceptance_criteria: Either ADR 0011 section 5 is amended and the model follows, or the bead is closed recording why the sentinel is preferred.
close_reason: ADR 0011 section 5 amended: quantity is NULL on a location label, enforced by label_quantity_iff_item, with a migration that nulls the existing sentinels.

title: Skill files restate DEVELOPERS.md instead of linking to it
description:
Found by the /simplify reuse pass. Pre-existing, not introduced by the QR work, so deliberately left out of that commit to keep it reviewable.

Both .agents/skills/*/SKILL.md declare they cover 'only conventions you cannot infer from those', then restate DEVELOPERS.md:
- react-frontend: the TypeScript typing policy (noExplicitAny / noNonNullAssertion) duplicates DEVELOPERS.md#code-style.
- django-backend: the @extend_schema rule duplicates DEVELOPERS.md#the-api-schema.
- Both Tests sections duplicate the DEVELOPERS.md#testing-and-coverage table almost line for line.

Per CLAUDE.md rule 1 the skills should keep only what is genuinely not inferable (e.g. the query-by-role rule, the manage.py path) and link for the rest.

Also noted: the 'no API URL baked into the bundle' explanation exists in three files (architecture.md, deployment.md, react-frontend skill); architecture.md should own it.
acceptance_criteria: Each duplicated topic has one owning document; the skills link rather than restate.
close_reason: Implemented in parallel worktrees, then reviewed and simplified once over the merged diff

title: Offline queue: replay a failed batch when the network returns
description:
Deliberately deferred out of the first release by decision 0011 section 12, not dropped. The two things that would have made it a rewrite - the client-side cart and the idempotency key - are being built now, so this is purely additive.

A service worker queues a failed batch and replays it when connectivity returns. Until then, retry-on-next-open covers most of the value and needs no browser API whose support has to be checked.
acceptance_criteria: A batch submitted with the network down is recorded exactly once when it returns; the queue survives a browser restart.

title: Revisit ty once it reaches 1.0
description: ty is pre-1.0 (0.0.72) and moving quickly. It currently type checks the backend cleanly including Django/DRF stubs. Re-evaluate at 1.0; mypy remains a drop-in fallback since the stub packages are already present and only the command in DEVELOPERS.md and CI would change. See docs/decisions/0004-python-tooling.md.
notes:
Concrete gaps to re-check at 1.0, all from implementing the catalogue models (inventory-tng-1p6):
- Reverse accessors (item.identifiers, volunteer.merged_from) report unresolved-attribute.
- django-simple-history managers (item.history) likewise.
- get_FOO_display() is invisible; we write Kind(self.kind).label instead.
All are django-stubs mypy-plugin features that ty does not run. Current workaround is documented in DEVELOPERS.md#typing. When ty gains plugin support, delete the '# ty: ignore[unresolved-attribute]' comments in backend/src/inventory/tests/test_models.py and re-check.
--- Re-check 2026-08-19: still pre-1.0, nothing removed ---

Version. ty's latest release is 0.0.73 (2026-08-19, github.com/astral-sh/ty/releases). The lock and the environment still resolve 0.0.72; pyproject pins ty==0.0.*, which is still correct. Astral announced Beta on 2025-12-16 (astral.sh/blog/ty) saying they were 'working towards a Stable release next year' -- that year is nearly over and the version is still 0.0.x, so 1.0 is not imminent.

All three gaps remain. Verified two ways against 0.0.73:
  * 'uv run --with ty==0.0.73 ty check --error unused-ignore-comment src' passes clean, i.e. every existing suppression is still doing work -- none has become unnecessary.
  * A scratch probe on 0.0.73 still reports unresolved-attribute for both get_kind_display() and a related_name reverse accessor.
django-simple-history managers follow from the same missing plugin, and the suppression on them is likewise still live.

Why it will not arrive via django-stubs. astral-sh/ty#291 ('Reimplement popular Mypy Plugins', which names django-stubs) is closed as not planned; a mypy-compatible plugin interface is explicitly out of scope. The Beta post lists 'first-class support for popular third-party libraries like Pydantic and Django' as a goal, so the fix has to be built into ty itself. Watch ty's release notes for Django support rather than watching django-stubs.

Scope has grown since this bead was written. Suppressions are no longer confined to tests/test_models.py: there are 20 across five files (models.py, views.py, serializers.py, tests/test_ledger.py, tests/test_models.py) and four rule codes, not one -- 17 unresolved-attribute plus one each of invalid-argument-type, invalid-method-override and unknown-argument. Only the unresolved-attribute ones are plugin-related; the other three are places a third-party stub is narrower than the function it describes, each already carrying a comment naming the stub, and Django support landing in ty will not remove them.

No files changed. DEVELOPERS.md#typing was checked line by line against the code and is still accurate, including its claim that the non-unresolved-attribute suppressions each explain which stub and why.
Astral targeted a stable ty for 2026; 2026-08-19 it is still 0.0.73 and all three gaps stand. Early January 2027 is the first checkpoint that can answer 'did the stable release they aimed at actually land', without churning through monthly 0.0.x bumps until then.
close_reason: Closed

title: Plan Django 6.1 -> 6.2 LTS upgrade before April 2027
description: Django 6.1 is a regular release with roughly a 16-month support window (chosen over 5.2 LTS deliberately). Django 6.2 is expected to be the next LTS in April 2027; schedule the upgrade rather than discovering it at EOL.
notes:
--- Plan written 2026-08-19: docs/briefs/django-6.2-upgrade.md ---

The plan lives at docs/briefs/django-6.2-upgrade.md and is linked from the Consequences section of docs/decisions/0003-django-version.md, which stays authoritative on why 6.1 was chosen. Nothing is duplicated between them.

Dates verified against djangoproject.com/download/ and the 6.1 release announcement (2026-08-05), not taken from this bead:
  * Django 6.1 released 5 Aug 2026. Mainstream support ends April 2027; EXTENDED (security) support ends December 2027.
  * Django 6.2 LTS expected April 2027, supported to April 2030. No Version6.2Roadmap wiki page exists yet, so April 2027 is a roadmap row and not a fixed day.

Correction to this bead. 'Before April 2027' conflated two different dates. April 2027 is when 6.2 arrives -- it opens the window. The deadline is December 2027, when 6.1 stops getting security fixes. The real drop-dead is four months later than this bead implied, giving an eight-month window.

New and material: the download page now states Django 6.2 is the FINAL release under the current versioning and support policy. From January 2028 Django uses YYYY versions released every January and every feature release gets the full three-year support period. That retires the LTS-versus-regular trade-off decision 0003 was written about; 0003's Consequences will describe a world that no longer exists. Flagged in the plan as a separate follow-up, not part of this upgrade.

What gates it (classifier survey as of 2026-08-19, in the plan as a table): drf-spectacular is the worst risk -- it declares only Django 6.0 and took ~7 months to support 6.0. django-simple-history and django-allauth are the other two to watch. django-cors-headers and whitenoise have 6.1 support merged but unreleased. psycopg and django-environ are effectively Django-version-agnostic.

Side finding, not acted on: django-stubs is pinned to 5.* and resolves to 5.2.9, so the type stubs describe Django 5.2 while the app runs Django 6.1. django-stubs 6.1.0 exists. The plan suggests folding the stub bump into this upgrade.

Repository exposure is low. The 6.1 deprecation timeline schedules NO removals for 6.2 -- everything deprecated in 6.0 and 6.1 is removed in the release after -- so 6.2 should be additive. backend/src uses none of the deprecated email settings/APIs, ADMINS/MANAGERS, StringAgg, BLANK_CHOICE_DASH or bare values_list(flat=True), and its one select_related() call passes field names. 'uv run pytest -W error::DeprecationWarning' surfaces no DeprecationWarning today.
Plan is written (docs/briefs/django-6.2-upgrade.md); nothing is actionable until Django 6.2 alpha exists. Django 6.1's alpha landed 2026-05-20 for a 2026-08-05 final, so a 6.2 alpha for an April 2027 final should appear in late January 2027. 2027-02-01 is the first date the 6.2 release notes and deprecation timeline can actually be read, and still two months ahead of the LTS and ten ahead of 6.1's December 2027 security EOL.
close_reason: Closed
